content.text: The text recounts Thomas Paine’s later life, religious writings, declining health, poverty, political disappointments, and posthumous reputation. In New York, he boarded with William Carver at 36 Cedar Street, later lived with the artist Jarvis, stayed with Hitt in Broome Street, and finally moved to Mrs. Ryder’s house and then William Thompson’s residence on Grove Street. He wrote essays attacking Christianity, defended Deism, and maintained his beliefs until death. His vote was refused at New Rochelle, and Congress rejected his claim for compensation. Friends disputed allegations that he was drunken, immoral, or neglected, attributing such charges to Carver and journalist James Cheetham. Paine died peacefully in Greenwich, New York, on June 8, 1809, and was buried on his New Rochelle farm after Quakers denied him burial. His remains were later exhumed by William Cobbett and taken to England. Appendices preserve Bonneville and John Hall’s recollections, while later material discusses gardening writers and landscape design.
